title: Pentagon adds ChatGPT Mil and Grok for Government to its GenAI.mil portal
subtitle: Custom OpenAI and xAI builds now sit alongside Google Gemini on the Department of Defense's central AI portal, which has onboarded 1.7 million of its 3 million personnel.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Department of Defense announced on August 31 that ChatGPT Mil and Grok for Government are now live inside GenAI.mil, the Pentagon's central portal for commercial AI models. The two builds — OpenAI's military-tuned ChatGPT and xAI's government edition of Grok, delivered through the Starshield channel — join Google Gemini, which has been on the portal since its launch last December. GenAI.mil covers roughly 3 million DoD personnel and has already onboarded about 1.7 million unique users. Access focuses on chat, files, projects, and custom GPTs for unclassified administrative, logistics, planning, and policy work.

The move matters because it settles, at least operationally, a question the DoD has been probing for two years: whether soldiers, analysts, and civilian staff can use frontier commercial models without those models quietly ingesting their prompts for training. The GenAI.mil versions are exempt from the consumer data-collection defaults that the same products apply on the open web, and the portal is the enforcement layer — the point of use where the DoD, not the vendor, controls what leaves the network.

The Pentagon inked $200 million ceiling contracts with Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and xAI in July 2025 to build these government editions. Today's announcement is the delivery: three of the four are now available to users, with Anthropic's Claude for Government still gated for reasons the department has not fully explained. The context is competitive as much as operational — every large model vendor now treats the U.S. government as an anchor customer, and being absent from the portal that 1.7 million federal employees actually log into is a market position, not just a procurement footnote.

Takeaway for learners: a general-purpose AI product and its 'government' or 'enterprise' variant are not the same system, and the difference is not just branding. Data handling, model versioning, tool access, and even the underlying weights can diverge — sometimes deliberately, sometimes as a side effect of how the vendor scopes access. If you are studying AI policy, procurement, or applied deployment, look past the model name on the login screen and ask which build is actually serving the prompt, what it retains, and who can see it.
